trackTitle: Java Core from Basic to Pro (Enterprise Edition)
description: A comprehensive, industry-standard Java Core learning roadmap from absolute beginner to enterprise architect & senior interview mastery level. Thoroughly covers Java syntax, object-oriented design, memory management, exception architectures, NIO.2, generics, Collections framework internals, high-performance multithreading, concurrency pipelines, Virtual Threads (Loom), functional programming (Lambdas, Streams, Collectors), JVM internals (ClassLoaders, JIT, G1/ZGC garbage collectors), JDBC data access, Gang of Four design patterns, and production-grade capstones.

segments.title: Segment 4 – Exception Handling & Robust Application Design (Intermediate - Advanced)
segments.summary: Build fault-tolerant Java applications: Exception hierarchy (Throwable, Error, Exception), Checked vs Unchecked exceptions, try-catch-finally execution semantics, throw and throws, Custom business exceptions, Try-with-Resources (ARM), and exception propagation.

modules.title: Exception Architecture: Checked vs Unchecked Exceptions
modules.summary: Understand Java's error handling philosophy: java.lang.Throwable root, Error (fatal JVM issues) vs Exception (recoverable errors), Checked exceptions enforced at compile-time vs Unchecked RuntimeExceptions.
topics: Why structured exception handling is superior to return-code error checking

java.lang.Error: unrecoverable system failures (OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError, VirtualMachineError)
java.lang.Exception: recoverable application-level conditions

Unchecked Exceptions (Runtime): subclasses of java.lang.RuntimeException (e.g. NullPointerException, ArithmeticException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, IllegalArgumentException, IllegalStateException)

modules.title: Try, Catch, Finally Blocks & Execution Flow

modules.title: Thread Fundamentals, Lifecycle & Creation
modules.summary: Understand the fundamentals of concurrency: Process (heavyweight) vs Thread (lightweight), thread memory (shared Heap vs private Stack), Thread lifecycle states (NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING, TERMINATED), extending Thread class, implementing Runnable, and Callable<V> with Future<V>.
topics: What is Concurrency vs Parallelism: multi-tasking on single-core vs true simultaneous execution on multi-core
Process vs Thread: address space isolation vs shared memory architecture
Thread Memory Architecture: shared Heap memory vs private per-thread Call Stack and PC Register
Thread Lifecycle & State Transitions in JVM (java.lang.Thread.State enum):
1. NEW: instantiated but not started
2. RUNNABLE: executing or ready to execute on CPU
3. BLOCKED: waiting to acquire an intrinsic monitor lock
4. WAITING: waiting indefinitely for another thread (wait, join)
5. TIMED_WAITING: waiting for a specified timeout (sleep, wait(t), join(t))
6. TERMINATED / DEAD: run method completed or threw unhandled exception
Creation Method 1: Extending java.lang.Thread class and overriding run()
Creation Method 2: Implementing java.lang.Runnable interface and passing to Thread constructor (Preferred)
Creation Method 3: Lambda expressions with Runnable (( ) -> { ... })
Creation Method 4: Implementing java.util.concurrent.Callable<V> to return values and throw checked exceptions
Starting a Thread: why we MUST call thread.start() instead of calling thread.run() directly
Thread naming and identification: Thread.currentThread(), getName(), setName(), getId()
Thread priorities (MIN_PRIORITY=1, NORM_PRIORITY=5, MAX_PRIORITY=10) and OS scheduling realities
learningOutcomes: Differentiate between processes and threads in operating system and JVM contexts
Trace thread state transitions across all 6 lifecycle states

commonMistakes: Calling run() directly instead of start(), executing the code synchronously on the caller thread

modules.title: Thread Control: sleep(), join(), yield(), interrupt() & Daemon Threads

Interrupting Threads: thread.interrupt(), thread.isInterrupted() (instance check), and Thread.interrupted() (static check + clear flag)

modules.title: Thread Synchronization: Synchronized Methods & Blocks
modules.summary: Eliminate race conditions on shared mutable state: Critical sections, the 'synchronized' keyword, Intrinsic Monitor Locks, Object-level locks (instance methods/synchronized(this)) vs Class-level locks (static synchronized methods/synchronized(Class.class)), and lock reentrancy.
topics: The problem of Shared Mutable State: Race Conditions and data corruption in concurrent access
Demonstrating the Classic Bank Account Balance Overdraw / Counter Increment Race Condition
Critical Section concept: code blocks accessing shared resources that must be executed by only one thread at a time
Java's Intrinsic Lock (Monitor Lock) attached to every Java object and class header
Synchronized Instance Methods: acquiring the intrinsic lock of 'this' instance
Synchronized Static Methods: acquiring the intrinsic lock of the 'Class' object (Class-level lock)
Synchronized Statements / Blocks: acquiring locks on specific lock targets (synchronized(lockObject) { ... })
Why Synchronized Blocks are preferred over Synchronized Methods: minimizing lock scope and contention
Object-Level Lock vs Class-Level Lock: detailed comparison and simultaneous non-interfering execution
Lock Reentrancy: why Java intrinsic locks are reentrant (a thread holding a lock can acquire it again without deadlocking)
Private Final Lock Objects: protecting lock targets from external interference (private final Object lock = new Object())

Differentiate between Object-level locks and Class-level locks in multi-threaded execution
Minimize lock scope using fine-grained synchronized blocks with private dedicated lock objects

High-Concurrency Thread-Safe Counter with Fine-Grained Block Synchronization

Locking on boxed primitive wrappers or String literals (which may be shared in string/integer pools)

modules.title: Inter-Thread Communication: wait(), notify() & Producer-Consumer
modules.summary: Coordinate thread signaling: wait(), notify(), and notifyAll() methods of Object class, IllegalMonitorStateException rules, spurious wakeups, loop condition checking, and implementing the classic Producer-Consumer bounded buffer.
topics: Why Inter-Thread Communication is needed: avoiding CPU-wasting busy waiting (polling loops)
The communication methods on java.lang.Object: wait(), wait(timeout), notify(), notifyAll()
Why wait/notify methods are declared in java.lang.Object instead of java.lang.Thread (locks belong to objects)
Mandatory requirement: wait() and notify() MUST be called inside a synchronized block holding that exact object's lock
IllegalMonitorStateException: causes and how JVM enforces lock ownership
How wait() works: releasing the intrinsic lock and placing the thread in the object's Wait Set
How notify() works: waking up a single arbitrary thread from the Wait Set and moving it to the Entry Set (Blocked for lock)
How notifyAll() works: waking up ALL waiting threads (preventing missed signals and thread starvation)
Spurious Wakeups: why threads can wake up without notification
The Golden Rule: ALWAYS call wait() inside a 'while' loop, NEVER inside an 'if' condition (`while (!condition) lock.wait();`)
Classic Problem: Building a Thread-Safe Bounded Buffer / Producer-Consumer Queue from scratch using wait() and notifyAll()
learningOutcomes: Coordinate complex asynchronous thread communication using wait, notify, and notifyAll
Prevent spurious wakeups and race conditions by embedding wait() inside while loops
Construct a production-quality Producer-Consumer bounded queue from scratch

Multi-Producer Multi-Consumer Print Job Spooler & Processing System

Using 'if' instead of 'while' before wait(), causing data corruption when multiple consumers wake up
Using notify() instead of notifyAll(), causing permanent thread starvation / signal loss

modules.title: Thread Safety, Deadlocks, Livelocks & Race Conditions
modules.summary: Diagnose and prevent catastrophic concurrency hazards: Race conditions (Check-Then-Act, Read-Modify-Write), Coffman Deadlock conditions, Deadlock detection with thread dumps (jstack/VisualVM), Lock Ordering rules, Livelocks, and Starvation.
topics: What constitutes Thread Safety: a class behaves correctly when accessed by multiple threads simultaneously
Categories of Race Conditions: Read-Modify-Write (counter++), Check-Then-Act (lazy initialization without synchronization)
What is a Deadlock: two or more threads permanently blocked, each waiting for a lock held by the other
The 4 Coffman Conditions required for a Deadlock:
1. Mutual Exclusion (non-shareable resources)
2. Hold and Wait (holding a lock while waiting for another)
3. No Preemption (locks cannot be forcefully confiscated)
4. Circular Wait (Thread A waits for B, B waits for A)
Breaking Deadlocks with Global Lock Ordering: acquiring locks in a consistent, globally deterministic sequence
Breaking Deadlocks with Timeouts (ReentrantLock.tryLock(timeout))
Simulating a classic Deadlock: The Dining Philosophers Problem and Bank Account Transfer deadlocks
Diagnosing Deadlocks in Production: capturing thread dumps with 'jcmd', 'jstack', and VisualVM
Analyzing thread dump stack traces to locate BLOCKED threads and deadlock cycles
Livelock: threads continuously changing states in response to each other without making forward progress
Thread Starvation: lower-priority threads perpetually denied CPU access or lock acquisition
learningOutcomes: Identify and eliminate subtle Read-Modify-Write and Check-Then-Act race conditions
Prevent deadlocks systematically by establishing global lock ordering rules
Capture and analyze JVM thread dumps to locate and resolve production deadlocks
miniProjects: Deadlock Detection & Prevention Simulator (Dining Philosophers Solution)
Production Thread Dump Analyzer & Deadlock Diagnosis Tool
commonMistakes: Acquiring multiple locks in different orders across different methods (e.g. transfer(A, B) locks A then B, while transfer(B, A) locks B then A)
Assuming race conditions only happen under high CPU load
references: Java Concurrency in Practice - Chapter 10: Avoiding Liveness Hazards

teachingTips: Create a live deadlock between two threads with Thread.sleep() and inspect it using `jstack <pid>` in terminal.

modules.title: Java Memory Model (JMM), `volatile`, Atomics & CAS
modules.summary: Understand hardware-level concurrency: Java Memory Model (JMM), CPU caches, instruction reordering, Happens-Before guarantee, the 'volatile' keyword (visibility vs atomicity), java.util.concurrent.atomic classes (AtomicInteger, AtomicReference), and hardware CAS (Compare-And-Swap).
topics: The modern CPU Architecture: L1/L2/L3 hardware caches, memory controllers, and main RAM
The Memory Visibility Problem: why changes made by Thread A in CPU Cache 1 may not be visible to Thread B in CPU Cache 2
Instruction Reordering: why compilers, JIT, and CPUs reorder instructions for performance without altering single-threaded semantics
The Java Memory Model (JMM) specification (JSR-133)
The 'Happens-Before' Relationship: formal rules guaranteeing memory visibility across threads
The 'volatile' keyword in Java:
- Guarantee 1: Memory Visibility (writes to volatile immediately flushed to main memory; reads read directly from main memory)
- Guarantee 2: Prevents Instruction Reordering (Memory Barriers / Fences)
Why 'volatile' does NOT guarantee Atomicity (e.g. volatile int count; count++ is still NOT thread-safe due to 3 bytecode operations)
Valid use cases for volatile: boolean status flags, double-checked locking singleton instance variable
Hardware CAS (Compare-And-Swap / Compare-And-Set): atomic CPU instruction (LOCK CMPXCHG)
Lock-Free Concurrency with java.util.concurrent.atomic package:
- AtomicInteger, AtomicLong, AtomicBoolean, AtomicReference
- Atomic methods: getAndIncrement(), incrementAndGet(), compareAndSet(expected, update), addAndGet()
High-Throughput Concurrency in Java 8+: LongAdder and DoubleAdder (striped cell counters minimizing CAS contention)

Apply the volatile keyword accurately to guarantee memory visibility without lock overhead

modules.title: ExecutorService, Thread Pools & CompletableFuture
modules.summary: Modern asynchronous Java engineering: java.util.concurrent.Executor framework, ThreadPoolExecutor architecture, standard thread pool flavors (Fixed, Cached, Single, Scheduled, WorkStealing), and asynchronous reactive composition with CompletableFuture.
topics: Why manual Thread creation (new Thread()) is an anti-pattern: thread creation overhead, unbounded thread exhaustion, lack of reuse

java.util.concurrent.Executor, ExecutorService, and ScheduledExecutorService interfaces

- Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n): fixed worker threads, unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue (OOM risk)

modules.title: Explicit Locks & Synchronizers: ReentrantLock, Latch, Barrier & Semaphore
modules.summary: Master explicit concurrency control: java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock, ReentrantReadWriteLock, Condition variables (await/signal), and concurrency synchronizers: CountDownLatch, CyclicBarrier, and Semaphore.

- orElse(fallbackValue): returns value or eager fallback

topics: Architectural overview of the Java Virtual Machine: ClassLoader Subsystem, Runtime Data Areas, Execution Engine, Native Interface (JNI), Native Method Libraries
The 3 Major Phases of the ClassLoader Subsystem:
1. Loading: reading binary .class bytes and creating java.lang.Class object in Metaspace
2. Linking:
- Verification: bytecode verifier checking binary format integrity and security constraints
- Preparation: allocating memory for static fields and setting default initial values (e.g. 0, null)
- Resolution: replacing symbolic references with direct memory references in runtime constant pool
3. Initialization: executing Static Initializer Blocks (SIB) and static variable initializers in source order
The Built-in ClassLoader Hierarchy:
- Bootstrap ClassLoader (C++ native core loader, loads java.base / rt.jar)
- Platform ClassLoader (formerly Extension ClassLoader)
- Application / System ClassLoader (loads classes from application classpath)
The Delegation-Parent Principle: why a ClassLoader always delegates loading requests up to its parent before attempting to load locally
Security benefits of Delegation-Parent model: preventing rogue replacement of core java.lang.String classes

topics: The 5 Runtime Data Areas of the Java Virtual Machine:
1. Method Area / Metaspace (Shared across all threads, Off-Heap in Java 8+)
2. Heap Area (Shared across all threads, stores all object instances and arrays)
3. Java Thread Stack (Private per thread, stores Stack Frames for method calls)
4. Program Counter (PC) Register (Private per thread, points to current executing instruction)
5. Native Method Stack (Private per thread, supports JNI C/C++ calls)

Metaspace memory management: native OS memory allocation, dynamic expansion, MaxMetaspaceSize
Deep Dive into JVM Heap Memory Architecture (Generational Model):
- Young Generation: Eden Space, Survivor Space 0 (From), Survivor Space 1 (To) (default ratio 8:1:1)
- Old / Tenured Generation: holds long-lived objects promoted after surviving N minor GC cycles (Tenuring Threshold)
- TLAB (Thread Local Allocation Buffer): thread-private heap allocation chunks eliminating synchronization lock contention during object creation
Deep Dive into Thread Stack Frames:
- Local Variable Table (LVT): storing primitives and object references
- Operand Stack: LIFO stack for bytecode arithmetic, evaluation, and method parameter staging
- Frame Data: runtime constant pool reference, normal method return completion, exception dispatch table

topics: The Principle of Garbage Collection: identifying unreferenced objects and reclaiming heap memory automatically
How JVM determines object liveness: Reference Counting (flawed, circular references) vs GC Roots Reachability Analysis (Tracing)

5. Shenandoah GC (-XX:+UseShenandoahGC): concurrent compaction ultra-low latency collector

- Heap sizing: -Xms4g, -Xmx4g, -Xmn2g (Young gen size)
- Metaspace sizing: -XX:MetaspaceSize=256m, -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=512m

topics: What is a Transaction: a single logical unit of work that must either completely succeed or completely fail
The ACID Properties in database systems:
- Atomicity: all or nothing execution
- Consistency: preserving database constraints and invariants
- Isolation: concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other
- Durability: committed changes are permanently saved even across system crashes
Managing Transactions in JDBC:
- Disabling auto-commit: connection.setAutoCommit(false)

Concurrency Phenomena in Multi-User Databases:
1. Dirty Read: reading uncommitted changes of another transaction
2. Non-Repeatable Read: reading different row data when re-querying due to another committed update
3. Phantom Read: reading a different number of rows when re-querying due to another committed insert/delete
The 4 Standard Transaction Isolation Levels in JDBC:
1. TRANSACTION_READ_UNCOMMITTED (permits dirty reads, highest throughput)
2. TRANSACTION_READ_COMMITTED (prevents dirty reads, default in PostgreSQL/Oracle)
3. TRANSACTION_REPEATABLE_READ (prevents dirty and non-repeatable reads, default in MySQL InnoDB)
4. TRANSACTION_SERIALIZABLE (prevents all anomalies, lowest concurrency, full lock/MVCC isolation)
Configuring Isolation Levels: connection.setTransactionIsolation(Connection.TRANSACTION_READ_COMMITTED)
